meta.title: Who really said "Every society honors its live conformists, and its dead troublemakers"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Wayne Dyer — Mignon McLaughlin wrote it in The Neurotic's Notebook (1963), p. 72. Dyer quoted a variant in 1999; McLuhan may have got it via a name mix-up.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every society honors its live conformists, and its dead troublemakers'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to Mignon McLaughlin's 1963 book The Neurotic's Notebook, page 72. Neither Wayne Dyer nor Marshall McLuhan created the saying.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1913–1983 · American journalist, magazine editor and aphorist
answer.sourceLine: The line is an aphorism by Mignon McLaughlin, published in The Neurotic’s Notebook (The Bobbs-Merrill Company, 1963), chapter 7, page 72 — a citation Quote Investigator verified with scans ↗. Wayne Dyer quoted a reworded version of it decades later; a 1999 newspaper reviewer credited that version to him, and the mistake stuck.

source.excerpt: Every society honors its live conformists, and its dead troublemakers.
trail: 1963 — the original. The aphorism appears in Mignon McLaughlin’s The Neurotic’s Notebook (Bobbs-Merrill, Indianapolis), chapter 7, page 72, reading “Every society honors its live conformists, and its dead troublemakers.” Quote Investigator gives this citation and reports it verified with scans ↗. The Internet Archive’s catalog record for that edition matches: Bobbs-Merrill, Indianapolis, 1963.
1981 — carried into the omnibus. The line is listed on Wikiquote’s Mignon McLaughlin page ↗ under The Complete Neurotic’s Notebook (1981), the collected edition — there without the 1963 comma.

1998–1999 — the Dyer detour. Wayne Dyer’s Wisdom of the Ages was published by HarperCollins in 1998 — per the Internet Archive’s catalog record ↗. QI’s evidence for the Dyer credit is not that book, though: Quote Investigator records only that a 1999 Gannett News Service reviewer quoted Dyer saying a slightly different version ↗: “Society honors its living conformists and its dead troublemakers.”

2004–2016 — the McLuhan drift. Quote Investigator documents misattributions to Marshall McLuhan across Usenet posts, tweets and online discussions in these years ↗, and suggests the error may hinge on confusion between the names McLaughlin and McLuhan.
source.excerptNote: The Neurotic’s Notebook is a collection of standalone aphorisms, not continuous prose — so this line has no surrounding sentence to quote. It sits as a single entry among the epigrams of chapter 7, which Quote Investigator places on page 72 ↗. Note the comma after “conformists” in the 1963 text; most circulating versions drop it.

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in The Neurotic’s Notebook in 1963 — well after the 1931 public-domain cutoff — so it should be treated as in copyright in the United States, not as a free-floating proverb. That the quote circulates unattributed on hundreds of quote sites has no bearing on its status: it is a short, identifiable literary aphorism by a named author with a named publisher. Quotle quotes it here briefly for identification and commentary.

author.name: Mignon McLaughlin
author.heading: Who was Mignon McLaughlin?
author.metaLine: 1913–1983 · American journalist, magazine editor and aphorist
author.bio: Mignon McLaughlin (1913–1983) was an American journalist who spent her career inside the mid-century magazine world — writing short stories for Redbook and Cosmopolitan, working at Vogue, and serving as copy editor and then managing editor of Glamour before retiring in 1973. Beginning in the 1950s she published the terse, mordant aphorisms that were later gathered into three collections known as the Neurotic’s Notebook books. Her epigrams travel far better than her name does: several of her best-known lines now circulate under more famous bylines, and this is one of them.

misattribution.heading: How Wayne Dyer ended up with it
misattribution.intro: This aphorism has drifted onto two famous men — one through a remark he made aloud to a reviewer, one possibly through a near-identical surname. Its actual author, a Glamour managing editor who died in 1983, is the one name most quote sites leave off.

items.why: Dyer’s Wisdom of the Ages (HarperCollins, 1998) was built around reflections on other people’s wisdom — which is exactly the kind of book that leaks quotations onto its author. Quote Investigator notes that a 1999 Gannett News Service reviewer quoted Dyer saying a variant of the line ↗ and readers took the speaker for the source. Dyer was born in 1940 — he was a young man when the line was already in print, and his own Wikiquote page contains no such quote at all ↗.

The more widespread error online. Quote Investigator tracks McLuhan misattributions from 2004 to 2016 and suggests the mechanism may be confusion between “McLaughlin” and “McLuhan” ↗. The split is still visible in the wild: Goodreads hosts the same sentence under McLuhan ↗ and under McLaughlin ↗ as two separate entries, neither citing a source.

The version attached to Dyer is not McLaughlin’s sentence. Quote Investigator records the Dyer-quoted form as “Society honors its living conformists and its dead troublemakers” ↗ — dropping “Every,” swapping “live” for “living.” QI also documents other drifting forms, including “The world values live conformists and dead rebels” and “Every age honours its dead rebels and living conformists.”

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion is unambiguous ↗: “Mignon McLaughlin should receive credit for the expression she crafted in her 1963 book. Neither Marshall McLuhan nor Wayne Dyer created this saying.”

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: Aphorism collections are the most attribution-fragile literature there is. A book like The Neurotic’s Notebook is ninety-six pages of unsourced one-liners with no argument around them to anchor a line to its author — every sentence is already formatted for the clipboard. Lift one out and nothing about it says “McLaughlin.” It just says quotable.

So the sentence went looking for a bigger name, and found two. Marshall McLuhan may have got it on a surname near-miss — Quote Investigator says the mechanism is uncertain. Wayne Dyer got it the way self-help authors usually do: he said it aloud to a reviewer in 1999, while promoting a book explicitly devoted to passing along other people’s wisdom, and the reviewer wrote down the man in front of him rather than the woman behind the line. Neither error required bad faith — only the ordinary friction of a good sentence moving faster than its citation.
detailsBody: McLaughlin’s 1963 text carries a comma before the final clause — “Every society honors its live conformists, and its dead troublemakers” — and that comma is doing real work. It puts a beat of hesitation before the turn, so “and its dead troublemakers” lands as an afterthought that detonates the first half of the sentence.
Nearly every version in circulation drops it, including the entry on Wikiquote ↗. It is a small loss, but it is the kind of erosion that marks a quotation’s distance from its page.
context.pull: The line survived. The byline did not.
